opus-5.5.text:
Context caching is one of the most important ideas for making agentic systems practical, and it's really a memory hierarchy problem.

In an agentic workflow you don't have one prompt and one answer. You have a long chain of model calls, tool calls, and more model calls, and much of the context gets reused across those steps: the system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents, and the growing history of what the agent has done. If you recompute the prefill for all of that on every step, you waste a huge amount of compute. And prefill is compute-bound, so it shows up directly in latency and cost. Context caching keeps the key-value state for that shared prefix so you only pay for the new tokens. When agents are making dozens or hundreds of calls, that's a big win.

The catch is that the KV cache is large, and it grows with context length, model size, and the number of concurrent agents. So the real question is where you keep it. HBM is fast but small and expensive. If the cache has to live there, you quickly run out of room, start evicting, and lose the benefit. That's why I think the right approach is a tiered memory system: HBM for active computation, a much larger capacity tier like DDR attached to the accelerator for warm context, and possibly storage beyond that. If you can move cached context between tiers quickly enough, you can keep many agents' contexts resident and switch between them without recomputing.

This connects to how we think about hardware. Agentic systems don't just need peak FLOPs. They need capacity and bandwidth to hold lots of state, and the ability to switch quickly between models and contexts. A dataflow architecture with a deep memory hierarchy is well suited to that, because you can orchestrate data movement explicitly rather than hoping a cache policy guesses right.

There are some caveats. Caching only works if prefixes are actually shared, so how you structure prompts matters. Put the stable material first and the variable material last, or you break reuse. Invalidation is also an issue: when tools return new information or the agent's plan changes, part of what you cached may no longer apply. And in multi-tenant settings you have to think about isolation between users' cached state.

Overall, I see context caching as essential, not optional. It turns a quadratic-feeling cost of agent loops into something closer to incremental. But to fully realize it, you have to co-design the software scheduling and the memory system in the hardware. That's where the interesting systems work is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says that fully realizing context caching requires co-designing software scheduling with the hardware memory system, and explains the need for a tiered memory hierarchy. This communicates that context caching alone is insufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think context caching is one of those ideas that sounds like a small systems optimization but actually tells you a lot about where the bottlenecks really are in agentic workloads. If you look at what an agent is doing, it's not a single prompt and a single response. It's this long, iterative loop. You've got a system prompt, you've got tool definitions, you've got the accumulated history of the task, and then at each step the model generates a relatively small amount of new text, calls a tool, gets a result back, and the whole thing goes around again. So the prefix of that context is overwhelmingly shared from one step to the next, and recomputing the attention over that prefix every single time is just wasted work. Caching the KV state for that shared prefix is the obvious thing to do, and it gives you real wins on both latency and cost, because prefill is where a lot of the compute goes for these long contexts.

Now, I come at this from a hardware and systems perspective, so the way I think about it is that context caching is really exposing a memory hierarchy problem. The KV cache for a long context is big. It's gigabytes per sequence for a large model, and you've got to decide where it lives. Does it stay resident in HBM on the accelerator? Do you spill it to host memory? Do you spill it further to some disaggregated storage tier? And then the question becomes what the access pattern looks like, how long these prefixes stay hot, how many concurrent agents are sharing the same prefix. That's a classic caching problem in the sense that we've studied in computer architecture for decades, with the same kinds of questions about locality, eviction, and bandwidth between tiers. What's different is that the objects are enormous and the reuse is structured in a very particular way by the shape of the agent loop.

So I'd say two things about how to assess it. First, it's clearly necessary, and anybody serving agentic workloads at scale who isn't doing it is leaving a lot on the table. Second, the current implementations are fairly coarse. Most of what's deployed is exact prefix matching, so if something changes early in the context, you lose the whole cache downstream of it. Agents are messy about that. They reorder things, they summarize, they inject tool results in the middle. There's a lot of room for smarter approaches, whether that's position-independent caching, or chunk-level reuse, or architectures where the hardware itself is designed around streaming that cached state in and out efficiently rather than assuming everything fits in one accelerator's memory. I think that's actually one of the more interesting places where the model architecture, the serving software, and the hardware design all have to be thought about together, which is the kind of problem I like.

r001.rationale: The response calls context caching necessary and describes limitations in current implementations, but it does not clearly state that context caching alone is insufficient.

astra-6.text:
I think context caching is useful, but it addresses only part of the problem. If an agent repeatedly uses the same instructions, documents, or conversation prefix, you can reuse the computation associated with that context. That reduces the cost of processing the input and can improve response latency.

But in an agentic system, the context is constantly evolving. You’re getting tool results, taking different paths, and updating what the agent knows. So the question becomes: how much of that context is actually reusable, and for how long? You also have to weigh the benefit of caching against the memory required to retain it.

I’d distinguish that from caching the result of an entire operation. Context caching lets you avoid some repeated computation, but the model still has to generate an answer. If you can safely reuse a previous result, you can potentially skip much more work. The challenge there is determining whether that result is still valid for the current request. So I see context caching as one useful layer in a broader caching strategy for agents.

r001.rationale: The response says context caching “addresses only part of the problem” and describes it as one layer in a broader caching strategy for agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think context caching is useful, particularly when you have a large amount of context that stays the same across multiple calls. You can avoid processing that same prefix over and over again, and that can reduce both latency and cost.

But in an agentic system, the context is evolving. You’re getting results back from tools, you’re making decisions, and those decisions affect what you do next. So the question is how much of that context you can actually reuse. If the shared material is at the beginning and the new information is appended, caching works well. If you keep changing the earlier context, you lose a lot of that benefit.

There’s also a memory tradeoff. Keeping those intermediate representations around consumes capacity, and moving them back into the system can become a bandwidth problem. So I’d view context caching as a useful part of the solution. You still have to look at the whole agent workflow and understand where the time and resources are going.

r001.rationale: The response calls context caching “a useful part of the solution” and says the whole agent workflow must be considered, communicating that context caching alone is insufficient.
